title: How Fresh Is Fresh
setting: a floodlit racecourse's three odds boards

post.author: u/floodlit_tote_babajide
post.title: I run the betting computers at a floodlit racecourse. A winning slip came to the pay window at 8/1, printed twenty seconds after the price was cut to 5/1. The punter's own screen had already shown him 5/1.

blocks.text: I'm Babajide, night tote operator at a floodlit racecourse: Thursday evening meetings, six races under the lights. We sell fixed-price bets: the price, or odds, printed on a slip is what it pays. 8/1 means 8 back for every 1 staked, plus the stake.
Prices live in a database, a computer that keeps records and answers questions about them. Ours has one main copy, called the leader. Only our trader changes prices, and only there.

The leader passes every change on to three more copies, called followers. In steps: the leader saves the change and gives it the next number; it sends it to each follower; each follower stores it, then shows it.
How far a follower trails the leader is called its lag. Ours is usually under 200 ms (thousandths of a second), far too little for anyone to see.

Each follower drives one big board. Asking a copy for a price is called a read, and our 120 betting terminals, the touch screens people bet on, make most of them. A terminal sends its reads in turn: the first to follower 1, the next to 2, then 3, then 1 again, so no copy does all the work.

Thursday 15 October, the 20:45. At 20:40:10 the trader cut number 6 from 8/1 to 5/1 after a run of bets on it: change 412. At 20:45, the off, betting closed with all three boards at 5/1. Number 6 won.

At 20:52 Remedios, our payout clerk, rang the tote room. Any winning slip at a longer price than the boards showed at the off goes in her query tray, and she checks its print time against the price log, the leader's list of every change. This one said 8/1, printed at 20:40:30: twenty seconds after the cut.
Twenty seconds after the cut, a terminal sold the old price.
The punter came up with her. He'd bet on terminal 17. Its runners screen said 5/1, its stake screen 5/1, and the confirm screen, the last before the slip prints, 8/1.
Terminal 17 keeps a diary of its screens. Each line: the time, the screen, which follower answered, the newest change it held, and number 6's price.

20:40:22  runners  follower 1  change 412  5/1
20:40:26  stake    follower 2  change 412  5/1
20:40:30  confirm  follower 3  change 411  8/1
20:40:30  slip printed at 8/1

Follower 3 was 25 seconds behind. On Monday our IT firm started a new nightly backup on it: a full copy of its disk, the part that stores its data, sent to their office. In steps: at 20:00 the job starts reading the whole disk; while it reads, each change from the leader waits its turn to be stored. Thursday was our first meeting since.

Board 3 showed 8/1 for those 25 seconds too. It stands at the far turn, across the track, and nobody can watch it and another board at once. If other screens went backwards that night, nobody said: only winning slips reach Remedios.

The leader turns green at 20:40:10, followers 1 and 2 at 20:40:10.2, follower 3 not until 20:40:35; from 20:40:10 to 20:40:35 its row is red. Markers: the cut at 20:40:10, the runners screen 5/1 at 20:40:22, the stake screen 5/1 at 20:40:26, the confirm screen 8/1 at 20:40:30, and follower 3 showing 5/1 at 20:40:35.

Red on follower 3 is the 25 seconds it still showed 8/1 after the cut, while the backup held its disk. The runners and stake screens read followers 1 and 2; the confirm screen at 20:40:30 read follower 3.

blocks.text: We paid it at 8/1: a printed slip is a promise. The backup stays at 20:00, the only slot the IT firm has. Next Thursday's 20:45 is our autumn feature, the busiest race of the year. What should we change before then?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: The promise a system makes about how fresh an answer is, when copies trail one another, is called a consistency model. Before you choose one, read terminal 17's diary again. Which copy answered each screen, and what was the newest change it held? By the confirm screen, what had that terminal already seen? And which answer did the slip's price come from?

replies.author: u/floodlit_tote_babajide
replies.text: Runners and stake: followers 1 and 2, change 412. Confirm: follower 3, change 411. By then terminal 17 had already shown change 412 twice, and the slip took its price from a copy 25 seconds old.

comments.author: u/catches_up_anyway_przemek
comments.text: Copies that may disagree for a moment but always agree once changes stop arriving: that's eventual consistency, and plenty of big sites run on it. Yours catch up in under a second on any normal night. The backup is the fault, not the design. Buy three bigger, faster followers so none falls behind again, and keep reading from all three.

replies.author: u/floodlit_tote_babajide
replies.text: The IT firm likes this one. New machines, nothing else to change.

comments.author: u/saved_copy_svetozar
comments.text: The trouble is three screens asking three different copies. Have each terminal keep its own saved copy of the prices, called a cache, and refill it every 30 seconds. Runners, stake and confirm then all read the same copy, so a punter never sees the price jump about.

reply.prompt: Next Thursday's 20:45 is the autumn feature, the busiest race of the year. What should the course change before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Give the three followers bigger, faster machines so they never fall behind the leader.
options.part2: On Monday 19 October the IT firm moved all three followers onto bigger, faster machines. With the backup running, follower 3 now trails by 4 seconds instead of 25. In the sim, replaying 15 October at 4 seconds behind: Thursday's punter, tapping 12, 16 and 20 seconds after the cut, sees 5/1 three times and is paid 5/1. A quicker punter, tapping 1, 2 and 3 seconds after the cut, sees 5/1 from follower 1, 5/1 from follower 2, then 8/1 from follower 3, and the slip prints at 8/1, a price cut 3 seconds before. On the feature night Remedios's query tray had slips in it again, each printed just after a cut.
options.senior: Faster followers shrink the lag; they don't change what a reader is promised. Reads in turn promise only that the copies agree eventually, so any two copies that are even a little apart can show one person a newer price and then an older one. A small lag makes the window rare, not impossible, and a backup, a busy disk or a slow network will open it again. The fix is a promise about order that the terminal keeps, not a hope about speed.

options.text: Serve a terminal no copy older than it has seen; check each bet's price on the leader.
options.part2: On Monday 19 October the IT firm changed the terminals and the betting program. Each terminal now remembers the newest change number it has shown; a follower holding anything older says no, and the terminal asks the next one. When a bet is placed, the terminal asks the leader for the price; if it has moved, the screen shows the new price and the punter confirms again. In the sim, replaying 15 October: runners 5/1 from follower 1 (change 412), stake 5/1 from follower 2, then follower 3, still at 411, says no and follower 1 answers 5/1. The leader confirms 5/1 and the slip prints at 5/1. The checks add 2 reads a second to the leader on an ordinary race and 40 on the feature, of the 1,000 it can answer. On 22 October the backup ran as usual, and every slip Remedios checked matched the price log.
options.senior: Two promises, each where it is needed. Screens need monotonic reads: once a terminal has shown change 412, it never shows anything older. That is cheap: the terminal remembers one number, any follower that has caught up can answer, and the reads stay spread over three copies. Money needs more: the price on a slip must be the price at that moment, and only the leader knows it for certain, so the bet is checked there, linearizable where money changes hands. The leader takes a few reads a second, not thousands. The costs are honest: a punter whose price moved must confirm again, and while the leader is down no bet can be taken.

options.text: Send every price read to the leader, so no terminal ever sees a price that is out of date.
options.verdict: Trade-off: fresh until the big race
options.part2: On Monday 19 October every terminal was pointed at the leader. In the sim, replaying 15 October: all three screens show 5/1 from the leader and the slip prints at 5/1. On ordinary races the leader takes 300 reads a second, of the 1,000 it can answer. Then the feature, on 22 October: 2,400 reads a second in the last minutes before the off, more than twice what the leader can answer. Screens waited in line, and the trader's price changes waited behind them: the one copy that can change a price was too busy answering questions about it.
options.senior: Reading only from the leader is linearizable and simple: every screen sees one up-to-date order. You pay in capacity, and at the worst moment: every read now lands on the one machine that must also take every change, and the busiest minute for reads is the busiest minute for price changes. Followers exist to spread reads, as the library's copies did. Keep the strong read for the few places that need it, like the bet itself, and give screens a cheaper promise from the followers.

options.text: Cache the prices on each terminal for 30 seconds, so screens and slips read the same.
options.part2: On Monday 19 October each terminal began keeping a saved copy of the prices, refilled every 30 seconds. In the sim, replaying 15 October: terminal 17 refilled its copy at 20:40:05, five seconds before the cut, so runners, stake and confirm all show 8/1, and the slip prints at 8/1, a price cut 20 seconds before. The screens now agree with each other and with nothing else: after every cut, any terminal can sell the old price for up to 30 seconds. On the feature night Remedios's query tray had slips in it again, each at a price the trader had already cut.
options.senior: A cache makes the screens agree by making them all equally old. Agreement between your own screens is not freshness: a 30-second cache turns a rare 25-second window on one follower into a window on every terminal after every cut. Saved copies are fine for things that rarely change and where old is harmless, like the race card; a price someone is paid on must be checked against the leader.

sim.title: Replay the minute around the cut
sim.lede: You're Babajide on Thursday 15 October 2026 at 20:40:00, ten seconds before the cut. As given data: the leader numbers every change; change 411 is the last before the cut, and change 412 at 20:40:10 cuts number 6 from 8/1 to 5/1. Followers 1 and 2 are 0.2 s behind; follower 3 is 25 s behind with the backup running, 4 s on bigger machines, 0.2 s on a normal night. Terminal 17's runners, stake and confirm screens each make one read: 12, 16 and 20 s after the cut as on Thursday, or 1, 2 and 3 s after it for a quick punter. In turn, they go to followers 1, 2 and 3. A saved copy on the terminal refills every 30 s, at 20:40:05 and 20:40:35. On an ordinary race the terminals make 300 reads and take 2 bets a second; on the feature race, 2,400 and 40. Saved copies refill 4 times a second across the 120 terminals. The leader can answer about 1,000 reads a second besides setting prices. Set where reads go, the check on the leader, the saved copy, follower 3's lag, the punter's speed and the load, then play 20:40:00 to 20:41:00.
sim.tryThis: Try this: play it as built: 5/1, 5/1, then 8/1 from follower 3, and the slip prints at 8/1, a price cut 20 s before. Send reads only to a follower at least as new as the last change seen, and turn the check on: follower 3 says no, follower 1 answers, the slip prints at 5/1, and the leader takes 2 reads a second (40 on the feature race). The leader only: 300 reads a second, then 2,400 on the feature race, swamped. Follower 3 at 4 s: fine at Thursday's pace, but a quick punter still sees 5/1, 5/1, 8/1. A 30-second saved copy: 8/1 on every screen and on the slip. The check alone: the screens still go backwards, but the slip prints at 5/1. Follower 3 at 0.2 s: nobody can see the gap.

explain.oneLine: No copy was broken. Terminal 17 read follower 1, then follower 3, which was 25 seconds behind, so one punter saw the price go backwards and was sold a price cut 20 seconds before. Screens need monotonic reads, never older than what you've already seen; money needs a linearizable check on the leader.

steps.title: Every follower is a little in the past.
steps.text: This is leader-follower replication, as in The Copy That Lags: one leader takes every change, and followers copy it in order, each a little behind; the gap is the lag. Followers that answer reads are read replicas, as in The Copy in the Back Room, where reads were spread over copies to spare the main one. In steps: first, the leader saves change 412 and numbers it. Second, it sends it to each follower. Third, each follower stores it, then shows it. What can go wrong: at the third step a busy disk makes a follower store late. On Thursday the backup held follower 3's disk, so at 20:40:30 it still showed the leader as it stood at 20:40:05.

steps.title: Reads in turn, and how one person went backwards.
steps.text: First, the runners screen asked follower 1 at 20:40:22: change 412, 5/1. Second, the stake screen asked follower 2: change 412, 5/1. Third, the confirm screen asked follower 3: still change 411, 8/1. Each answer was a true copy of the leader at some moment; the trouble is the order. Taking turns between copies that are behind by different amounts lets an older answer come after a newer one. With every follower under 200 ms behind, that gap is too short for a person to see; at 25 seconds it is long enough to place a bet in. Board 3 showed the same stale price, but a board has no memory of what you saw a moment ago, and nobody watched it.

steps.title: The ladder of promises.
steps.text: A consistency model is the promise a system makes about what a reader can see. From the strongest: linearizable means everyone sees one up-to-date order, as if there were a single copy; a read made after a change has finished always shows it. Causal means effects never appear before their causes: nobody sees the new prices made because a horse was withdrawn without also seeing the withdrawal. Session guarantees are promises to one reader, such as one terminal: read-your-writes (you always see your own changes) and monotonic reads (never older than what you have already seen). Eventual means only that copies agree once changes stop arriving. Reads in turn gave eventual consistency and nothing more, and it was kept: 25 seconds later, all three followers agreed.

steps.title: Monotonic reads, step by step, and a check where money changes hands.
steps.text: First, the terminal remembers the newest change number it has shown: 412, after the runners screen. Second, each read carries that number, and a follower answers only if it holds at least that change. Third, if it doesn't, the terminal asks the next follower. Like a cloakroom ticket, the terminal carries proof of what it has already seen and won't take less. What can go wrong: a terminal that restarts forgets its number, and a terminal whose very first read hits a stale follower is never warned. So the bet itself is checked on the leader, the one copy that is always up to date: linearizable at the moment money changes hands, and only there.

steps.title: Why the other fixes fail.
steps.text: Bigger machines shrink follower 3's lag to 4 seconds with the backup running, and a quick punter still sees 5/1, 5/1, 8/1. Reading only from the leader is always up to date, but the feature race's 2,400 reads a second swamp a leader that can answer about 1,000, and its price changes wait behind them. A 30-second saved copy makes every screen agree by making them all old: the slip still prints at 8/1. And eventual consistency was never broken that night; it simply promises too little for a price someone will be paid on.

diagram.aria: The fix replayed for Thursday 15 October. At 20:40:22 terminal 17 asks follower 1 for the runners screen and gets 5/1, change 412; it remembers 412 as the newest change seen. At 20:40:30 the confirm screen asks follower 3 for a copy at least as new as 412; follower 3 holds only 411 and says no. The terminal asks follower 1, which answers 5/1, change 412. When the bet is placed, the terminal asks the leader whether the price is still 5/1, and the leader says yes. Outcome: the slip prints at 5/1.

explain.caption: The fix, replayed for 15 October. Terminal 17 remembers change 412 from its runners screen (the stake screen, from follower 2, is the same and left out). At 20:40:30 follower 3, 25 seconds behind, refuses to answer with anything older, so follower 1 answers, and the bet's price is checked on the leader before the slip prints.

fix.title: The fix: monotonic reads for screens, a leader check for bets
fix.text: Keep reads spread over the three followers, but give each terminal a promise about order. The leader numbers every change and every answer carries its change number. The terminal remembers the newest number it has shown, sends it with each read, and a follower holding anything older says no, so the terminal asks the next one. That is monotonic reads, and it costs one number per terminal. Then, when a bet is placed, the terminal asks the leader for the price at that moment; if it differs from the screen, the screen shows the leader's price and the punter confirms again, and the slip always prints what the leader holds. Leave the boards on their followers, and add a lag alert so a follower more than a few seconds behind is seen the same night.

limits: Monotonic reads protect one terminal's own sequence. Two terminals side by side can still show different prices for a few seconds; that is allowed, and the check on the leader is what keeps it from costing money.
The check needs the leader. If the leader is down or cut off, no bet can be taken until it is back or a follower is promoted: the price of being sure at the moment money changes hands.
A terminal that restarts forgets the newest change it has seen. Save the number, or start from the leader's current number, or its first screen after a restart can be older than its last one before.

explain.seniorTake: "Fresh" is not one thing. A consistency model names which kind you are promised: linearizable (one up-to-date order, as if there were one copy), causal (effects never before causes), session guarantees such as read-your-writes and monotonic reads (one reader never goes back in time), and eventual (copies agree later). Spreading reads over followers with no promise gives you eventual, and a person can watch it run backwards. Choose per read: give screens a session guarantee, which followers can keep cheaply, and pay for linearizable only where a value decides money or a decision, by reading it from the leader or a majority at that moment. Making the followers faster narrows the window without changing the promise.

realWorld.title: Jepsen: linearizable, the strongest single-copy promise
realWorld.text: Jepsen's consistency models reference says "Linearizability is one of the strongest single-object consistency models", and that it means "every operation appears to take place atomically, in some order, consistent with the real-time ordering of those operations". Single-object means one record at a time, such as one horse's price. Atomically means all at once, never half done; real-time ordering is the order a wall clock would give. That is the bet check: the leader's answer at the moment of the bet is the price.

realWorld.title: Jepsen: the cost of linearizable
realWorld.text: On the same page: "This model cannot be totally or sticky available; in the event of a network partition" some copies must stop answering. A network partition is a split: copies that can't reach each other. That is limit 2: with the leader cut off, no bet can be checked.

realWorld.title: Jepsen: causal, effects after causes
realWorld.text: "Causal consistency captures the notion that causally-related operations should appear in the same order on all processes", and "though processes may disagree about the order of causally independent operations." A process here is one reader or writer, such as a terminal.

realWorld.title: Jepsen: monotonic reads, and why followers can keep it
realWorld.text: The monotonic reads page sums it up: "intuitively, reads cannot go backwards." And: "Monotonic reads can be totally available: even during a network partition, all nodes can make progress." A node is one machine in the group. This is why the followers can keep serving screens without asking the leader.

realWorld.title: Jepsen: the ladder
realWorld.text: The models page places the session promises below causal: "Causal implies writes follow reads and PRAM." and "PRAM implies monotonic reads, monotonic writes,and read your writes." (the missing space is on the page). Writes follow reads, PRAM and monotonic writes (your own changes are seen in the order you made them) are more session promises; anything causal also keeps monotonic reads and read-your-writes.

realWorld.title: Jepsen's MongoDB 3.6.4 analysis, 2018: promises depend on settings
realWorld.text: Jepsen tested MongoDB's causal consistency sessions, which claim read-your-writes and monotonic reads among their guarantees. The abstract says that "with MongoDB’s default consistency levels, CC sessions fail to provide the claimed invariants", and the tests "show that sessions prevent anomalies so long as user stick to majority reads and writes". CC is causal consistency; an invariant is a rule that must always hold. Test the promise with the settings you actually run.

asked: Linearizable against eventual consistency: what is the difference?
What are monotonic reads, and how do you provide them?
Where do you pay for strong consistency?
interview.answer: A consistency model is the promise about what a reader can see when data lives on several copies. Linearizable is the strongest: everyone sees one up-to-date order, as if there were a single copy, so a read made after a write has finished always shows it. Eventual is the weakest: copies agree once changes stop arriving, and until then a read can be stale, and reads spread over copies can even go backwards. Between them sit causal consistency, where effects never appear before their causes, and the session guarantees for one client: read-your-writes and monotonic reads. Monotonic reads means a client never sees anything older than it has already seen. I'd provide it in steps: the leader numbers every change and each answer carries its number; the client remembers the newest number it has seen and sends it with each read; a replica that hasn't reached it refuses or waits, and the client tries another, or the leader. Sticking each client to one replica also works until that replica fails. Strong consistency costs a trip to the leader or a majority, and that leader's capacity, so I pay for it only where a value decides money or an irreversible action: the price at the moment a bet is placed, stock at checkout, a balance before a withdrawal. Screens get monotonic reads from replicas. I'd tell the story of a racecourse whose terminals read three followers in turn: one was 25 seconds behind, a punter saw 5/1, 5/1, then 8/1, and the slip printed at the price cut 20 seconds before.

terms.def: The person who runs a racecourse's betting computers. The name comes from the totalisator, an older kind of betting machine; Babajide's course now sells fixed-price bets.
A bet paid at the price printed on the slip, whatever happens to the price afterwards.
What a winning bet pays: 8/1 means 8 back for every 1 staked, plus the stake. Also called the odds.
The person at the course who sets and changes prices, only ever on the leader.
Someone who places a bet.
The printed ticket for one bet: the horse, the price, the stake and the time it was printed.
The money placed on a bet. The stake screen is where the punter enters it, before the confirm screen.
The moment a race starts and betting on it closes. The 20:45 went off at 20:45.
A meeting's main race, which draws the most bets. On the feature race the terminals make about 2,400 reads a second.
The person at the pay window who pays winning slips. Remedios puts any slip at a longer price than the boards showed at the off in her query tray.
The leader's list of every change, with its number and time. Remedios checks a queried slip's print time against it.
One of the course's three big price displays. Each is driven by one follower; board 3 stands at the far turn.
A touch screen people bet on. The course has 120. Each bet passes through a runners screen, a stake screen and a confirm screen, and each screen makes one read.
A computer program that keeps records and answers questions about them. The course's prices live in one.
The one main copy of the prices. Only it takes changes, numbers each one and sends it on to the followers.
A copy that receives the leader's changes in order, stores them and answers reads. It takes no changes of its own. Also called a replica.
The number the leader gives each change, one more than the last. Change 412 cut number 6 to 5/1; change 411 came before it.
Asking a copy for a value, here a price. Each terminal screen makes one.
Sending each read to the next copy in a fixed order, 1, 2, 3, then 1 again, to share the work. Also called round robin.
How far a follower trails the leader. The course's is usually under 200 ms; on Thursday follower 3's was 25 seconds.
Short for millisecond: a thousandth of a second. 200 ms is a fifth of a second.
The part of a computer that stores its data for good. A follower writes each change to its disk before showing it.
A saved copy kept so data can be put back after a loss. The IT firm's new nightly backup reads follower 3's whole disk from 20:00.
Older than the leader's current value. Follower 3's 8/1 at 20:40:30 was stale by 20 seconds.
A reader seeing a newer value and then an older one, as terminal 17 showed 5/1 and then 8/1.
A saved copy kept close by so it can be read again quickly. A terminal cache of 30 seconds shows prices up to 30 seconds old.
The sim's terminal cache: refilled every 30 s, at 20:40:05 and 20:40:35 for terminal 17. Every screen reads it instead of a follower.
Asking the leader for the price when the bet is placed. If it differs from the screen, the screen shows the leader's price and the punter confirms again.
Asked for more than a machine can answer, so requests wait in line. The leader answers about 1,000 reads a second besides setting prices.
The promise a system makes about what a reader can see when data lives on several copies: from linearizable, the strongest, down to eventual.
Everyone sees one up-to-date order, as if there were a single copy: a read made after a change has finished always shows it. Reading from the leader gives it.
Effects never appear before their causes: anything that could have led to a change is seen before it, by everyone. Unrelated changes may be seen in different orders.
A promise to one reader, such as one terminal, about its own sequence of reads and writes: read-your-writes and monotonic reads are two.
Once you have changed something, your own later reads always show the change. Also called read-your-own-writes.
Once you have seen a value, you never see an older one. A terminal keeps it by remembering the newest change number it has shown.
Copies agree once changes stop arriving and have all been copied, but may disagree at any given moment.
A loose name for the stronger models, usually linearizable: reads always show the latest finished write.
Another name for a follower: a copy of the data that applies the leader's changes.
Keeping each reader on the same follower for every read, so what it sees only moves forward until that follower fails.
More than half of the copies: two of three. Reading or writing on a majority is one way to get the stronger models.
Turning a follower into the leader, usually because the old leader has failed.
An alert that fires when a follower is further behind than a set limit, such as a few seconds.
All at once, never half done: no reader can see an operation partly finished.
A split in the network: copies that can't reach each other for a while, each side still running.
One machine in a group of machines working as one system.
In Jepsen's pages, one reader or writer, such as one terminal, making operations one after another.
Jepsen's term: every copy can keep answering even when the network is split. Sticky available means the same, as long as each reader stays with one copy.
Two more session promises on Jepsen's ladder: PRAM, every reader sees one writer's writes in that writer's order; writes follow reads, a write lands after the writes its writer had read.
A project that tests databases under failures and publishes analyses of whether they keep their promises, plus a reference of consistency models.
A program that hands each incoming request to one of several machines, to share the work.
The program asking a database for data, such as a terminal or a phone app.
The small library an app uses to talk to a database. Some can be set to send reads to replicas.
A widely used database that stores records as documents. Jepsen analysed its version 3.6.4 in 2018.
MongoDB's causal consistency sessions: a client's reads and writes grouped so they keep causal order and the session guarantees.
A rule that must always hold, such as a reader never seeing an older value after a newer one.
In MongoDB, a write counts only once most copies hold it, and a read returns only data that most copies hold.
The processing integrity criteria in a SOC 2 report, an auditor's report on a company's controls: processing should be complete, valid, accurate and on time.

atWork: Look for reads spread across replicas with no session guarantee. It is a common pattern: a database driver, a proxy or a load balancer, a program that hands each request to one of several servers, sends each read to any replica in turn, and nothing remembers what a user has already seen. Ask three things. Can one user's two reads land on two replicas that are behind by different amounts, so a page shows a newer value and then an older one? Which reads decide money or an action that can't be undone, a price, a balance, stock at checkout, and are those read from the leader or a majority at that moment, or from whatever replica answers? And does anything alert you when a replica falls more than a few seconds behind? Give screens monotonic reads (a version or position the client carries, or a sticky replica), and send the few reads that decide money to the leader. Standards: if your company is pursuing a SOC 2 report that includes processing integrity (PI1), the price charged must be the price shown; decide which reads must be linearizable in the first design, not at audit time.

recall.prompt: Your shop's product pages read stock levels from three read replicas, taking turns. A customer sees '2 left', refreshes and sees '5 left', then checkout says 'out of stock'. Nothing is wrong with any one replica. What is going on, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: Reads taking turns over replicas that are behind by different amounts can show an older value after a newer one
Give each session monotonic reads: remember the newest version seen and read only from a replica at least that new, or keep it on one replica
Read the value that decides money from the primary at that moment: a linearizable read only where it matters

recall.model: The pages take turns between replicas that are behind by different amounts, so a newer answer ('2 left') can be followed by an older one ('5 left'): reads in turn give only eventual consistency, and here they went backwards. I'd give each session monotonic reads: remember the newest version it has seen and read only from a replica at least that new, or keep the customer on the same replica. And at checkout, where money changes hands, read the stock from the primary, a linearizable read, so the order is decided on the up-to-date value.

recall.prompt: In the sim, with everything else as built, which setting never shows terminal 17's price going backwards, always prints the slip at the leader's price, and keeps the leader coping on the feature race?
options: Follower 3 only 4 s behind, on bigger, faster machines
Every screen's read sent to the leader, and only the leader
Reads at least as new as last seen, plus the leader check
A 30-second saved copy of the prices on each terminal
recall.why: Only the last-change rule with the check passes all three: follower 3 says no, follower 1 answers 5/1, the leader confirms 5/1, and it takes 2 reads a second (40 on the feature race). At 4 s a quick punter still sees 5/1, 5/1, 8/1; the leader alone is swamped by 2,400 reads a second; the saved copy prints 8/1.

recall.prompt: Which promise is described by 'once you have seen a value, you never see an older one'?
recall.why: Monotonic reads is a session guarantee for one reader: it never goes back in time. Linearizable is stronger (one up-to-date order for everyone), causal keeps causes before effects, and eventual promises only that copies agree later.

recall.prompt: In an interview you're asked: what is the difference between linearizable and eventual consistency, and where would you pay for the strong one?

keyIdeas.idea: Linearizable: one up-to-date order as if there were a single copy; a read after a finished write always shows it
Eventual: copies agree only once changes stop; meanwhile reads can be stale or even go backwards
Pay for it only where a value decides money or an action, and give screens a cheaper session promise

recall.model: Linearizable means every reader sees one up-to-date order, as if there were a single copy: once a write has finished, every later read shows it, in real time. Eventual consistency only promises that copies agree once changes stop arriving; until then a read may be stale, and reads spread over copies can even go backwards. Linearizable costs a trip to the leader or a majority, and that one machine's capacity, so I'd pay for it only where money or an action depends on the value, like checking the price at the moment a bet is placed or the stock at checkout, and give screens a cheaper session promise, monotonic reads, from followers.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 4 months later. Since October no screen has gone backwards, and every slip Remedios has queried has matched the price log. In January the course launched a phone app for bets, which keeps the screens' rule: it never shows a copy older than the newest change it has read. On Thursday 4 February 2027 follower 2 was 6 seconds behind while the IT firm swapped a disk. At 20:12:03 a punter placed a bet on the app, and the leader took it. At 20:12:05 his 'my bets' page read follower 2, which didn't have it yet, so the page showed nothing. He placed it again. Two slips, one meant.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. The app never goes backwards, so why did his bet vanish from his own page, and what should change?

keyIdeas.idea: The app only remembered changes it had read; his write went to the leader and its change number was never remembered
Read-your-writes: remember the change number the write returns and read only from a copy at least that new, or from the leader
Monotonic reads and read-your-writes are separate session guarantees; the app needs both

coldCase.model: Monotonic reads only promise never to show anything older than what the app has read, and the app had never read his bet: the leader took his write, but the app didn't remember the write's change number, so follower 2, 6 seconds behind, still counted as new enough. That is a separate promise, read-your-writes. When the leader takes a bet it should send back the bet's change number; the app remembers the highest number it has written or read, and reads 'my bets' only from a copy at least that new, or from the leader. Both are session guarantees, and a betting app needs both.
